title: Scientific or Technological Uncertainty - SR&ED Glossary
description: Understand Scientific or Technological Uncertainty in our Canadian SR&ED glossary and why resolving it is vital for R&D tax credit eligibility.
summary: Scientific or technological uncertainty is the first test of SR&ED eligibility in Canada: under the Income Tax Act and the Northwest Hydraulic five-question test, Canadian businesses claiming SR&ED investment tax credits must show a technological risk that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures, define the baseline knowledge, and describe it on Form T661, Line 242.

Executive Overview and the 2024–2026 Legislative Transformation

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program serves as the cornerstone of Canada's federal industrial and innovation policy, delivering non-dilutive fiscal support to enterprises conducting systematic scientific and technological investigation within Canadian jurisdiction. Administered jointly through legislative policy established by the Department of Finance Canada and operational enforcement executed by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the regime operates through a dual-benefit statutory mechanism embedded within the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) and the Income Tax Regulations. Qualifying taxpayers obtain both an immediate or indefinitely carryforwardable deduction against business income under subsection 37(1) and an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under sections 127 and 127.1 that reduces federal Part I tax payable or yields a direct cash refund.

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential structural modernization since the 2012–2014 austerity reforms. Recognizing that declining business enterprise R&D intensity and historical capital expenditure exclusions were eroding national productivity, the Department of Finance initiated a two-phase public consultation process beginning on January 31, 2024. Phase one ran until April 15, 2024, examining program architecture, eligibility definitions, intellectual property retention, and international competitiveness alongside a parallel consultation on a domestic patent box regime. On April 16, 2024, the federal government tabled Budget 2024: Fairness for Every Generation, launching a second consultation phase running through May 27, 2024, and committing $600 million over four years commencing in 2025—with $150 million per year on an ongoing basis—to enhance the SR&ED framework.

The technical parameters of this reform were unveiled in the federal Fall Economic Statement tabled on December 16, 2024, and subsequently expanded in Budget 2025 tabled on November 4, 2025. On November 18, 2025, the Minister of Finance and National Revenue tabled Bill C-15, An Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1). Following passage by the House of Commons on February 26, 2026 and third reading in the Senate, Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 as S.C. 2026, c. 3. Retroactively effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024), Bill C-15 enacted four foundational transformations: doubling the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3.0 million to $6.0 million; broadening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million while introducing an elective gross revenue phase-out alternative; extending access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs); and reinstating the pre-2014 eligibility of capital expenditures for both the subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the section 127 ITC.

Complementing the legislative overhaul enacted by Bill C-15, the CRA launched a formal, optional pre-claim approval process on April 1, 2026, providing businesses with binding upfront eligibility determinations within eight weeks of application via My Business Account prior to incurring project costs. Subsequently, Budget 2026 proposed an additional $930 million expansion of the SR&ED program specifically targeted at domestic commercialization and intellectual property retention, paired with the Productivity Mega Deduction for immediate capital expensing and the Canada Growth Incentive providing up to a $15 million capital gains exemption on qualifying small business shares. Simultaneously, provincial jurisdictions—most notably Quebec through its March 25, 2025 consolidation of fragmented R&D credits into the universal Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), as well as Ontario and Alberta through targeted capital expenditure adjustments—realigned their sub-national regimes with the modernized federal baseline.

body.text: Statutory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
The Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

The legal gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Unlike tax regimes that evaluate eligibility based on commercial novelty or market differentiation, subsection 248(1) establishes a strictly scientific and technological standard. It defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and classifies qualifying activities into three primary pillars, coupled with enumerated supporting activities and explicit statutory exclusions.

Under this statutory framework, the first primary pillar is basic research under paragraph 248(1)(a), which encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. The second pillar is applied research under paragraph 248(1)(b), which covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third and operationally most significant pillar is experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c), defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. In Canadian corporate tax practice, over 90% of industrial SR&ED claims are filed under the experimental development branch of paragraph 248(1)(c). Complementing these three core categories, paragraph 248(1)(d) admits eligible supporting work—specifically work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude from the definition of SR&ED any work with respect to market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection. Furthermore, Budget 2025 clarified effective November 4, 2025, that expenses incurred for determining the quality of a mineral resource in Canada do not include expenses related to determining the economic viability or engineering feasibility of the mineral resource. A critical second-order implication of this statutory architecture is that supporting activities—such as software coding, CAD modelling, or laboratory testing—cannot qualify on a standalone basis; their eligibility is entirely derivative of, and strictly proportional to, an underlying basic research, applied research, or experimental development project that seeks to overcome a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty.
The Subsection 37(1) Deductible Expenditure Pool

The first statutory incentive of the SR&ED program is governed by section 37 of the Income Tax Act. Normally, under section 9 and paragraphs 18(1)(a) and 18(1)(b) of the Income Tax Act, business expenses are deductible only to the extent they are incurred for the purpose of gaining or producing income, while outlays on account of capital are non-deductible except as amortized through Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) under paragraph 20(1)(a). Subsection 37(1) overrides these general limitations by establishing a specialized, cumulative tax pool—the "pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures"—for SR&ED carried on in Canada.

Under paragraph 37(1)(a), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may include in the subsection 37(1) pool all expenditures of a current nature made in the year on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, as well as qualifying payments to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or other similar institutions to be used for SR&ED related to the taxpayer's class of business. Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, paragraph 37(1)(b) was restored for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, allowing capital expenditures to be pooled and deducted immediately at 100% in the year the property becomes available for use. Furthermore, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) permit a taxpayer to include permissible salaries and wages paid to Canadian-resident employees for SR&ED carried on outside Canada, subject to a strict statutory ceiling of 10% of the total salaries and wages paid for SR&ED carried on in Canada during the taxation year.

The balance in the subsection 37(1) pool at the end of a taxation year is computed by adding current-year allowable expenditures (plus any repayments of prior government assistance) and subtracting government assistance, non-government assistance, super-allowance benefit amounts under paragraph 37(1)(d.1), contract payments received, and the prior-year federal SR&ED ITC claimed or refunded (which is recaptured into the pool reduction under paragraph 37(1)(e) or included in income under paragraph 12(1)(t) if the pool goes negative). A crucial strategic feature of subsection 37(1) is that deducting from the pool is entirely discretionary: a taxpayer may deduct any portion of the positive pool balance in the current taxation year to reduce net income for tax purposes, or leave the balance undeducted to carry forward indefinitely into future taxation years (subject to acquisition-of-control streaming restrictions under subsection 37(6.1)). This indefinite carryforward preserves the tax value of R&D deductions for pre-revenue startups without triggering the 20-year expiry clock that governs ordinary non-capital losses under paragraph 111(1)(a).
The Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit Framework

The second and financially predominant pillar of the federal regime is the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC), governed by subsections 127(5) through 127(35) and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act. Subsection 127(9) defines "qualified expenditure" as an expenditure incurred by a taxpayer in a taxation year that is an expenditure described in paragraph 37(1)(a) or (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) paragraph 37(1)(b), plus the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) where elected under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, less prescribed excluded expenditures, non-qualifying unpaid amounts (under subsection 127(26) when unpaid 180 days after year-end), government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments.

Under subsection 127(5), a taxpayer may deduct its available ITC pool to offset federal Part I tax otherwise payable. Where the generated ITC exceeds Part I tax payable—or where the claimant is in a tax-loss position—section 127.1 governs the calculation of the "refundable investment tax credit," deeming the refundable portion to be a payment on account of the taxpayer's Part I tax liability and thereby generating a direct cash refund from the Receiver General for Canada. Because any ITC claimed (whether used to offset Part I tax or received as a cash refund) reduces the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year (or triggers an income inclusion under paragraph 12(1)(t) if the pool is exhausted), the federal SR&ED ITC is effectively taxable in the year following its claim, creating a one-year timing deferral on the taxback of the credit.
Enacted Federal Rates, Expenditure Limits, and Phase-Out Mechanics
Enhanced 35% Refundable Credit and the $6 Million Expenditure Limit

Canadian income tax law bifurcates the SR&ED ITC into two rate tiers: an enhanced 35% rate designed for domestic small- and medium-sized innovative corporations, and a general 15% rate applicable to all other claimants and excess expenditures. Prior to the 2024–2026 reforms, the enhanced 35% rate was strictly limited to qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) on up to $3,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures per taxation year, yielding a maximum annual refundable credit of $1,050,000.

While the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit to $4,500,000, Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 (enacted via Royal Assent on March 26, 2026) superseded that figure by raising the annual SR&ED expenditure limit to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Consequently, a qualifying corporation with at least $6,000,000 in eligible current SR&ED expenditures can now generate up to $2,100,000 in 100% refundable federal SR&ED ITCs annually—doubling the non-dilutive cash flow ceiling available under the legacy framework. Under subsection 127(10.3), corporations that are associated with one another (as determined under section 256 of the Income Tax Act) must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit across the associated corporate group and file a prescribed allocation agreement on Schedule 49 (Form T2SCH49) with their T2 returns.
Dual Phase-Out Regimes: Taxable Capital Versus Gross Revenue Elections

A critical policy advancement enacted by Bill C-15 is the overhaul of the expenditure limit phase-out mechanics for CCPCs. Under the legacy subsection 127(10.2) formula, a CCPC's $3,000,000 expenditure limit was ground down on a straight-line basis when the taxable capital employed in Canada (within the meaning of Part I.3, section 181.2) of the corporation and its associated group for the immediately preceding taxation year lay between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000. (Whereas Budget 2019 previously eliminated the prior-year taxable income phase-out test for federal SR&ED purposes, leaving only taxable capital as the federal phase-out metric prior to Bill C-15, Ontario continues to enforce a taxable income grind for the provincial OITC).

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 introduces a dual-track phase-out architecture for CCPCs that combines an expanded taxable capital range with an elective gross revenue alternative. Under the default expanded taxable capital test, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to phase out only when the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and its associated group exceeds $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated only when taxable capital reaches $75,000,000. Expressed mathematically, for a CCPC with a full 365-day taxation year using the taxable capital method where TC represents prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada (in dollars), the expenditure limit is determined as follows:
Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A = 0 if TC ≤ $15,000,000, and otherwise A = the lesser of $60,000,000 and (TC − $15,000,000)
Under this linear formula, each $10 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1.

Alongside the expanded taxable capital range, Bill C-15 introduces an elective gross revenue phase-out regime operating over the identical $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 corridor. Recognizing that venture-backed technology, biotechnology, and clean-energy CCPCs frequently raise substantial equity or convertible debt financing—which inflates balance-sheet shareholder equity and debt (and thus Part I.3 taxable capital employed in Canada) long before the company generates commercial revenue—Bill C-15 allows a CCPC to formally elect to compute its expenditure limit phase-out using the three-year average gross revenue structure rather than taxable capital. Under this election, a pre-revenue or early-revenue CCPC with $80,000,000 in venture capital equity on its balance sheet but only $5,000,000 in average annual gross revenue preserves its entire $6,000,000 expenditure limit and full $2,100,000 refundable ITC entitlement. Conversely, a mature, high-revenue, asset-light software CCPC with $60,000,000 in gross revenue but only $8,000,000 in taxable capital can remain on the default taxable capital test to retain its full $6,000,000 expenditure limit, allowing each CCPC to select whichever statutory metric yields the higher expenditure limit.
Inclusion of Eligible Canadian Public Corporations under Subsection 127(10.6)

Prior to Bill C-15, a Canadian corporation that completed an initial public offering (IPO) or reverse takeover on a public stock exchange—such as the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX), TSX Venture Exchange (TSXV), or Canadian Securities Exchange (CSE)—immediately lost its CCPC status under subsection 125(7) and was relegated to the 15% non-refundable ITC rate. This statutory cliff penalized domestic capital formation and incentivized premature foreign acquisitions.

Through Bill C-15's amendments to subsection 127(10.1), the new definition in subsection 127(9) and the enactment of subsection 127(10.6), Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) are now granted full access to the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy four cumulative statutory criteria throughout that year. First, the corporation must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year. Second, a class of its shares must be listed on a designated stock exchange, or the corporation must have validly elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation under subsection 89(1). Third, the corporation must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (encompassing both de jure and de facto control under subsection 256(5.1)), by one or more non-resident persons. Fourth, the corporation would not be controlled by a single person if every share of its capital stock owned by a non-resident person (determined, absent actual knowledge, on the basis of publicly available information, including information filed under securities laws before the year) were owned by that one person. An eligible subsidiary of such a corporation may also qualify as an ECPC.

For an ECPC (or a CCPC electing the gross revenue method), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis when the average annual gross revenue of the corporation (and its associated corporate group, determined on a consolidated basis in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles) over the three preceding taxation years falls between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. Denoting the three-year average gross revenue as GR, the statutory phase-out is calculated as follows:
Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A = 0 if GR ≤ $15,000,000, and otherwise A = the lesser of $60,000,000 and (GR − $15,000,000)

For both CCPCs and ECPCs, if the taxation year is a short taxation year (fewer than 51 weeks or 365 days), the resulting expenditure limit is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365.
General 15% Credit, Carryback, and Carryforward Rules

Qualified SR&ED expenditures that do not qualify for the enhanced 35% rate—including expenditures incurred by a qualifying CCPC or ECPC in excess of its $6,000,000 (or phased-out) expenditure limit, as well as all expenditures incurred by large public corporations, foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries, individuals, and trusts—earn the general federal SR&ED ITC rate of 15%.

The refundability of the ITC under section 127.1 depends strictly on the claimant's legal classification, the ITC rate tier, and whether the underlying expenditure is current or capital in nature. For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs claiming within the 35% rate tier, ITCs earned at the enhanced 35% rate on current expenditures are 100% refundable, whereas ITCs earned at the enhanced 35% rate on restored capital expenditures (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) are 40% refundable, yielding an immediate 14.0% cash refund alongside a 21.0% non-refundable tax credit component. Where a qualifying CCPC or ECPC incurs qualified expenditures above its expenditure limit (or is partially phased out but remains a qualifying corporation), the 15% ITC earned on those excess expenditures (both current and capital) is 40% refundable. Similarly, unincorporated businesses—specifically individuals (sole proprietors) and qualifying trusts—earn the 15% ITC, of which 40% is refundable. By contrast, for non-qualifying corporations, including large CCPCs or ECPCs exceeding the $75,000,000 phase-out threshold and all foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries, the 15% ITC is 0% refundable (strictly non-refundable).

To the extent that an SR&ED ITC is non-refundable (or the claimant elects not to claim the refund where applicable) and exceeds the claimant's federal Part I tax payable for the current taxation year, subsection 127(5) and paragraph 127(9)(a) permit the unused ITC balance to be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years to recover prior federal Part I tax paid, or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to offset future federal Part I tax liabilities.

body.text: Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Elections, and Restoration of Capital Property
Direct Salaries, Wages, and Permissible Foreign Activities

Salaries and wages represent the largest expenditure component of Canadian SR&ED claims. Under clause 37(1)(a)(i) and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, salaries or wages (as defined in subsection 248(1) to mean income from an office or employment under sections 5 to 8, plus the employer's share of statutory payroll deductions including Canada Pension Plan [CPP], Quebec Pension Plan [QPP], Employment Insurance [EI], Quebec Parental Insurance Plan [QPIP], and provincial workers' compensation boards) are 100% eligible to the extent that the employee is directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

CRA administrative policy and Regulation 2900 distinguish between employees who are "directly engaged" in hands-on technical SR&ED work (including first-line technical supervisors who direct the scientific investigation, formulate hypotheses, and evaluate experimental outcomes) and general administrative or executive personnel. Where an employee spends 90% or more ("all or substantially all") of their total working time in the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages may be included in the claim. Where an employee spends less than 90% of their time on SR&ED, only the exact proportion of time directly engaged in eligible SR&ED activities may be claimed, substantiated by contemporaneous time-tracking records or labour allocation matrices.

Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), salaries or wages incurred for SR&ED carried on outside Canada are eligible only if the work is performed by an employee who is a resident of Canada, the work is directly undertaken by the taxpayer (not a foreign subcontractor) as an integral part of a core Canadian SR&ED project, the remuneration is not subject to a foreign income or profits tax, and the total foreign salary claim does not exceed 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada in the year.
Specified Employees and Statutory Remuneration Caps

To prevent owner-managers from artificially shifting corporate profits into refundable 35% SR&ED tax credits via year-end bonuses, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose stringent restrictions on specified employees. Under subsection 248(1), a "specified employee" of a person is an employee who is a "specified shareholder" of the employer—meaning a taxpayer who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, not less than 10% of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any corporation related to the corporation—or an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, child, or sibling of a controlling shareholder).

For any specified employee, three cumulative statutory limitations govern eligible remuneration. First, there is a total prohibition on bonuses and profit-based remuneration: unlike arm's-length employees (whose bonuses and taxable benefits are includable in direct SR&ED wages under the subsection 37(1) pool, though excluded from the proxy salary base), a specified employee cannot claim any bonus, remuneration based on profits, or taxable benefit under sections 6 or 7 for SR&ED purposes. Second, the overall direct SR&ED salary or wages claimable for a specified employee in a taxation year is subject to a statutory ceiling of 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was employed by the corporation. Associated corporations employing the same specified employee must share this ceiling and file an allocation agreement on Form T1174. Third, when the taxpayer elects the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method for overhead, subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the Income Tax Regulations further restrict the amount of a specified employee's salary that can enter the proxy salary base to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total eligible salary or wages (excluding bonuses and taxable benefits) for the year and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated for the number of days employed in the year. Consequently, even if a founder-CTO spends 100% of their working time on hands-on experimental development, while up to 100% of their salary (capped at 5x YMPE) is eligible as direct SR&ED wages, at most 75% of their salary (capped at 2.5x YMPE) can generate the 55% notional overhead proxy.
Overhead Allocation: Prescribed Proxy Amount Versus Traditional Method

Taxpayers claiming SR&ED must elect annually on Line 160 of Form T661 between two mutually exclusive methodologies for capturing SR&ED overhead and other expenditures: the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method or the Traditional Method. Once filed for a taxation year, this election is statutorily irrevocable for that year.

Under the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method, rather than tracking, itemizing, and substantiating actual overhead costs, the claimant calculates a notional overhead amount equal to 55% of the SR&ED salary base pursuant to subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations. (A frequent compliance error in outdated literature is citing a 65% proxy rate; the rate was 65% up to 2012, transitioned to 60% in 2013, and has been fixed at 55% since January 1, 2014). Under subsection 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations, the salary base comprises the portion of salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, strictly excluding taxable benefits (under sections 6 and 7), bonuses, remuneration based on profits, deemed subsection 78(4) unpaid remuneration, and amounts exceeding the subsection 2900(7) and 2900(8) caps for specified employees. Furthermore, the overall PPA is subject to an overarching statutory cap under subsection 2900(6) to ensure that total deducted business expenses do not exceed actual business outlays.

Crucially, the PPA is a notional construct that exists solely for the purpose of computing "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) to generate federal (and harmonizing provincial) Investment Tax Credits. The PPA is never added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, actual overhead expenses (such as office rent, utilities, and administrative support salaries) remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the Income Tax Act. Moreover, because the 55% PPA statutorily replaces all overhead and "other expenditures directly attributable" to SR&ED, a taxpayer electing the PPA method is barred from separately claiming cloud computing costs, software-as-a-service (SaaS) subscriptions, shop supplies, or clerical support wages on Form T661, as doing so would constitute double-counting.

Under the Traditional Method, no notional proxy is calculated; instead, the taxpayer must itemize, track, and substantiate actual overhead and other expenditures that are both directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada and incremental—meaning the costs would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not been carried out. While the PPA method is overwhelmingly favoured by software and engineering firms where direct technical salaries dominate the cost structure, the Traditional Method has become increasingly strategic for artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and data analytics enterprises whose incremental cloud compute, GPU cluster rental, and specialized data-hosting expenses exceed 55% of their eligible Canadian SR&ED salary base.

body.text: Arm's-Length and Non-Arm's-Length Subcontractors and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant engages an independent, arm's-length subcontractor to perform SR&ED work in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool, but only 80% of the eligible contract payment may be included in "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) for the purpose of calculating the federal ITC. This statutory 20% haircut—enacted effective January 1, 2013—is designed to strip out the contractor's assumed commercial profit margin from the tax credit base. To substantiate an arm's-length contractor claim, the claimant must retain contracts and itemized invoices demonstrating that the work satisfied the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED (or directly supported the claimant's SR&ED under paragraph 248(1)(d)), that the work was physically performed within Canada (offshore subcontractor work is 100% ineligible), and that the claimant retained ownership or exploitation rights to the resulting intellectual property.

Where SR&ED is subcontracted to a non-arm's-length person (such as a parent, subsidiary, or sister corporation), the 80% rule does not apply, and the contract payment itself is not directly a qualified expenditure to the payer. Instead, the non-arm's-length performer may either claim the underlying eligible SR&ED costs directly on its own return or transfer the qualified expenditures (capped at the contract amount) to the non-arm's-length payer by jointly executing and filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), while any associated government assistance may be allocated between non-arm's-length parties using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length).

In addition to direct subcontracts, third-party payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D corporations for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to the taxpayer's class of business (where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results) are reported on Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) and are similarly subject to the 80% inclusion rate for federal ITC calculation purposes.
Materials Consumed or Transformed

Under subsection 37(1) and Regulation 2900(2)(a), the cost of materials is 100% includable in both the subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base if the materials are either materials consumed (rendered virtually value-less or destroyed) or materials transformed (incorporated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom test rig) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. General office supplies, laboratory glassware that is reused across multiple projects, and raw materials converted into commercial inventory for immediate sale without undergoing experimental uncertainty do not qualify as SR&ED materials. However, where an experimental prototype or custom-built pilot asset initially qualifies as materials transformed, and the taxpayer subsequently sells the prototype commercially or converts it to commercial production use, specific SR&ED recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(35) claw back the lesser of the ITC originally earned on the materials and the ITC rate multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value upon conversion), adding the recaptured ITC directly to the taxpayer's federal Part I tax payable in the year of sale or conversion.
Reinstatement of Capital Expenditures and Recapture Mechanics

Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures (depreciable property) and capital lease costs were completely excluded from both the subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the section 127 ITC. Enacted into law by Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the pre-2014 capital expenditure rules have been fully reinstated for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, as well as for lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024 (provided that, for leased equipment, the underlying capital expenditure was made by the lessor/performer after December 15, 2024).

To qualify as an eligible SR&ED capital expenditure under reinstated paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9), the depreciable property must become "available for use" (within the meaning of subsections 13(26) to 13(32)) in the taxation year and must satisfy one of two statutory intent tests at the time of acquisition. Under the operating time test, the property must be intended to be used all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time throughout its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Alternatively, under the value consumption test, all or substantially all (90% or more) of the value of the property must be intended to be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

Examples of qualifying capital property include specialized R&D laboratory instruments, environmental test chambers, tooling and moulds used 90% or more for experimental prototyping, and dedicated on-premises server and GPU hardware acquired for AI model architecture research. Statutorily excluded from SR&ED capital eligibility are land, buildings (other than a prescribed leasehold interest in a building used for SR&ED), goodwill, and property acquired prior to December 16, 2024.

While qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn the enhanced 35% ITC on eligible capital expenditures within their $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the refundability of capital ITCs is capped at 40% (yielding a 14.0% cash refund and a 21.0% non-refundable tax offset), whereas current expenditures within the limit enjoy 100% refundability. Furthermore, if a taxpayer subsequently sells SR&ED capital property or converts its use to commercial or non-SR&ED operations, statutory recapture rules apply under both section 13 (recovering claimed CCA/subsection 37(1) deductions) and subsections 127(27) to 127(35) (recovering previously claimed SR&ED ITCs as an addition to Part I tax payable).
Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payment Grinds

To prevent double-dipping across public funding programs, paragraph 37(1)(d) and the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) require claimants to reduce their SR&ED expenditure pool and ITC qualified expenditure base by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED at the time the tax return is filed.

Under subsection 127(9), "government assistance" means assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance—other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself. Consequently, direct innovation grants and non-repayable contributions—such as funding from the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF), Canada's Global Innovation Clusters, the NRC AI Assist Program, or provincial innovation agencies—directly reduce the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure base dollar-for-dollar on Line 515 of Form T661 to the extent they fund eligible SR&ED costs. Similarly, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (such as the Ontario OITC/ORDTC, Quebec CRIC, Alberta IEG, and British Columbia SR&ED credit) constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and must be deducted on Line 513 of Form T661, reducing the federal qualified expenditure base in the current year.

Conversely, unconditional repayable loans, bona fide equity investments by Crown corporations at fair market terms, and general tax rate reductions do not constitute government assistance, though low-interest or interest-free government loans may generate a benefit or assistance component depending on their statutory terms (and super-allowance benefit amounts under paragraph 37(1)(d.1) are likewise ground down). When a taxpayer repays government assistance or a contract payment in a subsequent year that previously reduced its qualified expenditures, the repayment (reported on Line 560 of Form T661) is added back into the subsection 37(1) pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base in the year of repayment.
Administrative Governance, Prescribed Forms, and Statutory Filing Deadlines
Institutional Roles of the Department of Finance and the Canada Revenue Agency

Canada's SR&ED ecosystem is characterized by a clear institutional separation between legislative design and operational administration. The Department of Finance Canada holds exclusive jurisdiction over tax policy, statutory amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations, budget allocations, and economic impact evaluations. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the program at the federal level (and administers harmonized provincial R&D credits on behalf of all participating provinces and territories except Quebec and Alberta, which administer their corporate tax systems independently through Revenu Québec and Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration, respectively).

Within the CRA's SR&ED Directorate, claims undergo a bifurcated review process integrating scientific evaluation with tax accounting verification. The technical review is conducted by CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs)—specialists holding advanced degrees and industrial experience in engineering, computer science, life sciences, chemistry, or manufacturing—who evaluate whether the claimed project narratives and contemporaneous technical evidence satisfy the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED and the Northwest Hydraulic five-question test. Concurrently or sequentially, the financial review is conducted by CRA Financial Reviewers (FRs), who audit the general ledger, T4 payroll summaries, specified employee ownership structures, subcontractor agreements, proof of payment, overhead elections, and government assistance reductions under section 37, section 127, and Regulation 2900.
Prescribed Federal Tax Forms and Technical Narrative Architecture

Pursuant to subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer cannot deduct an expenditure under subsection 37(1) or claim an ITC under section 127 unless the taxpayer files prescribed forms containing prescribed information with the Minister on or before the statutory reporting deadline. Following the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the CRA released updated versions of all core SR&ED forms and Guide T4088 (Guide to Form T661, revision t4088-26e.pdf) in May 2026. Filing on an outdated version of Form T661 can delay processing or result in administrative rejection.

At the centre of a federal SR&ED claim is Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), which is structured across 10 distinct parts. Part 1 captures general corporate and claimant identification, including the business name, tax year, and Business Number. Part 2 houses the project data and technical narratives, where for each claimed project the technical lead must answer three strictly word-capped narrative boxes demonstrating compliance with subsection 248(1). Specifically, Line 242 (capped at a maximum of 350 words) asks, "What scientific or technological uncertainties did you attempt to overcome?", requiring the claimant to define the baseline state of scientific or technological knowledge at the outset of the project, articulate why standard practice or routine engineering was insufficient, and specify the exact system-level or component-level technological uncertainty. Next, Line 244 (capped at a maximum of 700 words) asks, "What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainties described in line 242?", requiring a chronological account of the systematic investigation that details the specific hypotheses formulated, the experiments or analyses executed, the quantitative or qualitative metrics observed, how hypotheses were modified in response to test failures, and which portions of the work were performed by employees versus contractors. Finally, Line 246 (capped at a maximum of 350 words) asks, "What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve or attempt to achieve as a result of the work described in line 244?", requiring the claimant to articulate the new scientific or technological knowledge generated relative to the initial baseline, noting that under CRA policy and Tax Court jurisprudence, the failure of an experiment to reach its commercial or practical objective still constitutes a valid technological advancement if it conclusively proves why a hypothesized approach cannot work within specific technical constraints. Part 2 also includes the mandatory checklist of contemporaneous supporting evidence (Line 270 to Line 282) retained by the claimant.

The financial schedules of Form T661 begin in Part 3, which computes allowable SR&ED expenditures segmented by current versus capital costs, Canadian versus permissible foreign wages, and the Traditional versus Prescribed Proxy overhead election on Line 160, culminating in the subsection 37(1) deductible pool. Part 4 calculates qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes, incorporating the PPA, applying the 80% factor to arm's-length contracts and third-party payments, deducting provincial government assistance on Line 513 and other assistance on Line 515, reporting current SR&ED expenditures on Line 557, total qualified SR&ED expenditures including capital on Line 559, and assistance repayments on Line 560. Parts 5 through 10 encompass the calculation of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Part 5), project-by-project cost breakdowns (Part 6), statistical background data (Part 7), the claim completeness checklist (Part 8), mandatory disclosure of external SR&ED claim preparers and whether their billing arrangement involves a contingency fee (Part 9), and authorized corporate officer certification (Part 10).

To translate qualified expenditures from Form T661 into actual tax credits, corporations must file Schedule T2SCH31 (Schedule 31, Investment Tax Credit – Corporations), while unincorporated individuals file Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit – Individuals). Schedule 31 computes the 35% and 15% ITC amounts, expenditure limits, carrybacks, carryforwards, and refundable credits, with current-year allowable corporate ITCs reported at Line 540 and the total ITC refund flowing to Line 780 of the T2 return. Notably, Schedule 31 also serves as the central corporate reporting schedule for Canada's Clean Economy ITCs, including the Clean Hydrogen ITC (Line 140), Clean Technology ITC (Line 155), Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC (Line 170), Clean Electricity ITC (Line 185), and Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS) ITC (Line 200). Where associated corporations share the $6,000,000 expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.3), they must also file Schedule T2SCH49 (Schedule 49, Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit), alongside any applicable ancillary forms: Form T1145 (non-arm's-length assistance allocation), Form T1146 (non-arm's-length qualified expenditure transfer), Form T1174 (associated corporation specified employee salary allocation), and Form T1263 (third-party payments).
The Mandatory 18-Month Reporting Deadline and Absence of Ministerial Discretion

One of the strictest statutory traps in Canadian tax law is the SR&ED reporting deadline codified in subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. A taxpayer must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information for a specific expenditure on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date under section 150 for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred.

For a taxable corporation, paragraph 150(1)(a) sets the T2 income tax return filing-due date at 6 months after the end of its taxation year; adding the 12-month SR&ED reporting window yields a strict, non-negotiable deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the SR&ED expenditures were incurred. For example, a corporation with a December 31, 2025 taxation year-end has a T2 filing-due date of June 30, 2026, and an absolute SR&ED reporting deadline of June 30, 2027. For individuals carrying on a business, paragraph 150(1)(b) sets the T1 return due date at June 15 of the following calendar year, making the SR&ED reporting deadline 12 months later on June 15 of the second following year, or 17.5 months after the December 31 calendar year-end. For trusts, paragraph 150(1)(c) sets the T3 return due date at 90 days after the trust's taxation year-end, resulting in an SR&ED reporting deadline of 12 months plus 90 days after the trust's year-end. Conversely, under subsection 37(11), a corporation that is exempt from tax under section 149 and incurs SR&ED expenditures must file Form T661 on or before its T2 filing-due date (6 months after year-end) to avoid late-filing penalties.

Crucially, pursuant to subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act, the Minister of National Revenue's discretionary power under subsection 220(2.1) (to waive the filing of a prescribed form) and subsection 220(3) or 220(3.1) (the taxpayer relief provisions) does not apply to a prescribed form, receipt, or document, or to prescribed information, that is filed with the Minister after the 18-month period specified in subsection 37(11) or paragraph (m) of subsection 127(9). There is zero statutory mechanism or judicial discretion to extend the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline. If a corporation files its claim on Month 18 and Day 1—or files a timely claim at Month 6 but attempts to amend Form T661 to add an omitted project or omitted expenditure line item after Month 18—the claim or added expenditure is statutorily barred by operation of law.
The CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process and Complementary Federal Innovation Initiatives

To address long-standing industry concerns regarding post-filing audit uncertainty, the CRA officially launched its modernized Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026. Under this optional administrative mechanism, eligible businesses can submit a streamlined project application through the CRA's My Business Account portal before commencing experimental work or incurring R&D expenditures. The CRA reviews the proposed project against the subsection 248(1) criteria and issues a formal pre-claim approval determination within eight weeks, enabling corporate finance and engineering teams to commit R&D capital with upfront certainty regarding project eligibility. Additionally, the CRA retired and archived outdated sector-specific guidance—such as the former guidelines for SR&ED claims made by physicians and medical professional corporations—consolidating its administrative focus around the universal Eligibility of Work Policy.

Alongside the SR&ED program, the federal government deployed a comprehensive suite of complementary direct funding and tax measures during the 2024–2026 cycle. In the realm of sovereign artificial intelligence and compute infrastructure (Budget 2024 and the 2024 Fall Economic Statement), the government committed $2.4 billion across a multi-tiered AI package: $2.0 billion for the AI Compute Access Fund and Canadian AI Sovereign Compute Strategy, $200 million delivered through Canada's Regional Development Agencies to accelerate AI commercialization and adoption, $100 million for the National Research Council's (NRC) AI Assist Program helping small- and medium-sized enterprises build and deploy AI solutions, and $50 million for workforce transition alongside the establishment of the AI Safety Institute of Canada.

To further stimulate capital investment, Budget 2024, Bill C-15, and Budget 2026 introduced aggressive capital cost allowance (CCA) incentives. Businesses were granted full 100% immediate expensing for productivity-enhancing assets—specifically patents or rights to use patented information (Class 44), data network infrastructure equipment (Class 46), and general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and systems software (Class 50)—acquired on or after April 16, 2024 and available for use before January 1, 2027. This was followed by the five-year extension of the Accelerated Investment Incentive (AII) through 2033 under Bill C-15 and the introduction of the Productivity Mega Deduction in Budget 2026. Finally, to strengthen domestic intellectual property and entrepreneurial capital retention, the government allocated $14.5 million over two years to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) Innovation Asset Collective, maintained ongoing support for the $2-billion Global Innovation Clusters, expanded section 44.1 small business share rollovers under Bill C-15 (removing the historical common-share restriction and raising the eligible small business corporation carrying-value asset limit from $50 million to $100 million), and introduced the Budget 2026 Canada Growth Incentive providing a $15 million capital gains exemption for qualifying shares alongside a $930 million SR&ED commercialization expansion.

body.text: Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal Stacking

Every Canadian province (except Prince Edward Island, which delivers R&D support solely through direct grants rather than a statutory corporate income tax credit) and the Yukon Territory operates a dedicated sub-national R&D tax credit regime that stacks on top of the federal SR&ED program. While most jurisdictions piggyback directly on the federal subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED and are administered by the CRA via T2 supplemental schedules, Quebec and Alberta maintain autonomous corporate tax statutes and independent revenue administrations, and Ontario operates a dual-credit architecture.
Ontario: Innovation Tax Credit and Research and Development Tax Credit

Corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario that perform eligible SR&ED in the province can access two complementary corporate income tax credits administered by the CRA on behalf of the Ontario Ministry of Finance. The primary incentive for small- and medium-sized corporations is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566, which provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit for qualifying CCPCs on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures per taxation year, yielding a maximum annual cash refund of $240,000 (reduced from the 10% rate and $300,000 maximum that applied to taxation years ending before June 1, 2016). Unlike the federal SR&ED expenditure limit (which expanded to $6.0 million under Bill C-15 and eliminated the taxable income grind in 2019), Ontario retained its $3,000,000 expenditure limit and a dual phase-out mechanism: the $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is shared among associated corporations and is gradually reduced on a straight-line basis when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Crucially, Ontario updated the OITC rules to harmonize with the federal restoration of capital expenditures: the OITC qualified expenditure base includes 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024, whereas capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 and before December 16, 2024 remain excluded.

Complementing the OITC is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508, which provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures with no expenditure limit. Available to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment—including qualifying CCPCs (on both their OITC-eligible base after deducting the OITC entitlement and on expenditures exceeding the $3,000,000 OITC cap) as well as large, profitable, public, or foreign-controlled corporations that are ineligible for the OITC—the ORDTC is calculated by taking gross eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures, subtracting relevant government assistance (including any OITC claimed for the year), and multiplying the net base by 3.5%. Unused ORDTC credits can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable. Additionally, Ontario provides a 20% refundable Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) on qualifying contract payments to eligible Ontario research institutes.
Quebec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Consolidation and E-Business AI Reforms

Quebec operates an entirely independent corporate tax system under the Taxation Act (Quebec), administered by Revenu Québec in coordination with the Ministère des Finances du Québec and the Ministère de l'Économie, de l'Innovation et de l'Énergie. Historically, from 2008 until March 25, 2025, Quebec's R&D landscape was fragmented across four distinct refundable tax credits—the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D), the Tax Credit for University Research or Public Research Centres, the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research, and the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium—offering rates between 14% and 30% based on corporate asset levels ($50 million to $75 million) and subject to a complex per-employee exclusion threshold.

In the Quebec Budget 2025–2026 tabled on March 25, 2025, the Quebec government enacted a sweeping structural consolidation, abolishing the former R&D salary, university/public research centre contract, pre-competitive partnership, consortium fee (subject to transitional fee balance rules through December 31, 2029), technological adaptation services, and in-house industrial design tax credits (while leaving the fashion design component unchanged), and replacing them with a single, unified flagship incentive: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025.

The CRIC regime establishes a universal two-tier refundable rate structure that eliminates the legacy asset-based rate reductions ($50 million to $75 million in assets) and provides a 100% refundable credit to all corporations regardless of size or foreign ownership: 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures in excess of the exclusion threshold, and 20% on all eligible expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 limit (which must be shared among associated corporations). Beyond traditional R&D harmonized with federal SR&ED, CRIC extends 30%/20% refundable coverage to pre-commercialization activities performed in Quebec, explicitly encompassing regulatory testing and certification processes, product design and industrial design, technological validation, pilot production, prototype refinement and testing, and market studies required for commercialization. Aligning with federal Bill C-15, CRIC also restores eligibility for capital expenditures on R&D laboratory equipment, software development infrastructure, specialized prototyping machinery, and testing and validation equipment acquired for use in Quebec (subject to recovery via a special tax or limitations where property is used in a large investment project holiday).

Under CRIC, the first dollars spent annually below the statutory exclusion threshold do not generate a credit; the modernized exclusion threshold is calculated as the greater of $50,000 or the basic personal amount under the Quebec personal income tax system (for instance, $18,571 per employee in 2025) multiplied by the number of employees and prorated according to each employee's time devoted to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. For example, a Quebec corporation with 10 full-time R&D employees in 2025 faces an exclusion threshold of $185,710 ($18,571 × 10), earning the 30% credit on the first $1,000,000 above $185,710 and 20% on the remainder. Furthermore, for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025, Quebec reformed its Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE), adding data processing and hosting activities to specifically promote the eligibility of artificial intelligence businesses (CDAEIA) while removing routine software maintenance and evolution activities.
Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant and Post-Bill C-15 Adjustments

Following the elimination of the former 10% Alberta SR&ED tax credit on January 1, 2020, the Government of Alberta enacted the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) effective January 1, 2021, under Division 7 of Part 6 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, administered independently by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA). Delivered through the Alberta corporate tax system without requiring a separate grant application, the IEG is claimed by filing AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29), AT1 Schedule 13, and Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Carried Out in Alberta) with the corporation's Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (AT1). (Mandatory electronic Net File applies to all AT1 returns for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2024).

The IEG employs a hybrid base-plus-incremental rate structure on up to $4,000,000 in annual eligible Alberta R&D spending (shared among associated corporations via the prescribed agreement on page 3 of Form AT29), providing a maximum annual refundable grant of $800,000. Specifically, the grant provides a base 8% refundable payment on eligible R&D expenditures carried out in Alberta up to the corporation's "base amount"—defined as the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta R&D expenditures over the two immediately preceding taxation years—and an incremental 12% refundable payment (for an enhanced 20% combined payment) on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the two-year average base spending level, up to the $4,000,000 expenditure cap. To target small- and medium-sized enterprises, the calculated IEG is multiplied by a phase-out factor based on the corporation's (or associated group's) prior-year federal taxable capital employed in Canada (from Line 690 of federal Schedule T2SCH33) between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000:
Phase-out factor = 1 − [(TC − $10,000,000) ÷ $40,000,000], where TC is prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada and the factor equals 1 where TC ≤ $10,000,000
Corporations with $50,000,000 or more in prior-year taxable capital, as well as partnerships, trusts, and individuals, are completely ineligible for the IEG.

A critical technical compliance rule arose in 2026 following the federal enactment of Bill C-15. Because Alberta did not adopt the federal restoration of capital expenditures for IEG purposes, Alberta TRA issued updated Form AT29 (TRA14637 Rev. 2026-06) and Information Circular IEG-1R4 instructing claimants that for taxation years ending before December 16, 2024, the starting point on Line 003 of Form AT29 is Line 559 of federal Form T661, whereas for taxation years ending after December 15, 2024, claimants must use Line 557 of federal Form T661 (which reports only federal current SR&ED expenditures, excluding restored post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures reported in Line 559). Moreover, completing Form AT29 requires a mandatory two-step iterative calculation: Step 1 computes a preliminary IEG before provincial assistance, and Step 2 feeds that preliminary IEG into Line 513 of federal Form T661 to determine the final net Alberta eligible expenditures and net IEG (reported on Line 134 of Form AT29 and Line 129 of the AT1 return). TRA does not disburse IEG refunds until the underlying federal SR&ED expenditures have been verified by the CRA.
British Columbia and Other Provincial and Territorial Regimes

Across the remaining Canadian jurisdictions, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits harmonize with the federal SR&ED framework and are administered by the CRA. In British Columbia, corporations claim the provincial incentive on Form T666 (British Columbia Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit) within 18 months of taxation year-end, earning a 10% refundable tax credit for qualifying CCPCs on up to $3,000,000 of eligible BC SR&ED expenditures (subject to prior-year taxable income and taxable capital phase-outs), and a 10% non-refundable credit for other corporations and excess expenditures. Among the Atlantic, Prairie, and Territorial regimes, New Brunswick provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit for all corporations, and the Yukon Territory provides a 15% refundable R&D tax credit (plus an additional 5% on eligible payments to Yukon University). Similarly, Nova Scotia (15% refundable), Newfoundland and Labrador (15% refundable), Manitoba (15% credit, partially refundable for in-house R&D and fully refundable for eligible institute contracts), and Saskatchewan (10% refundable for CCPCs on the first $1 million and 10% non-refundable above) offer substantial regional stacking incentives that must be accounted for as government assistance on Line 513 of federal Form T661.
Inter-Jurisdictional Stacking, Transfer Pricing, and the Assistance Grind

Because provincial R&D tax credits reduce the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure base as government assistance under subsection 127(9), the combined federal-provincial effective tax credit rate is not simply the arithmetic sum of the statutory rates, but follows the multiplicative grind formula:
Combined credit rate = Provincial credit rate + [Federal ITC rate × (1 − Provincial credit rate)]

For example, in Ontario, a qualifying CCPC claiming both the 8% refundable OITC and the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC on its first $3,000,000 of current SR&ED expenditures (with the ORDTC calculated on the base net of OITC: 3.5% × (1 − 8%) = 3.22%, yielding a total Ontario credit of 8% + 3.22% = 11.22%) has its federal qualified expenditure base reduced to 100% − 11.22% = 88.78% of gross eligible spend. Applying the 35% federal refundable ITC to that net base (35% × 88.78% = 31.073%) produces a combined federal-Ontario credit of 42.293% before accounting for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount on direct labour. When the 55% PPA is applied to direct Canadian SR&ED salaries (42.293% × 1.55 ≈ 65.55%), the effective cash recovery per dollar of direct engineering salary exceeds 65% in Ontario and can exceed 70% in Quebec under the 30% CRIC plus 35% federal SR&ED stack.

For foreign-owned multinational subsidiaries operating R&D centres in Canada (which earn the 15% non-refundable federal ITC alongside provincial credits such as Ontario's 3.5% ORDTC or Quebec's 30%/20% refundable CRIC), proper accounting for federal and provincial R&D tax credits is essential in cross-border transfer pricing arrangements (further scrutinized under the modernized transfer pricing rules enacted in section 247 by Bill C-15). Where a Canadian subsidiary performs contract R&D for a foreign parent on a cost-plus basis, the CRA and foreign tax authorities examine whether the cost base charged to the foreign parent must be reduced by Canadian federal and provincial R&D tax credits, directly impacting inter-company service charges and deferred tax asset valuations on public financial statements.

body.text: Judicial Precedents, Burden of Proof, and Audit Defence Jurisprudence
The Cornerstone Five-Question Test in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants

While subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act provides the statutory text for SR&ED, its practical interpretation in every CRA audit, administrative objection, and judicial appeal is governed by the seminal Tax Court of Canada decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (T.C.C.). In that ruling, then Judge (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman synthesized the statutory requirements of subsection 248(1) into five cumulative criteria—universally known in Canadian tax jurisprudence as the "Five Questions"—each of which must be answered in the affirmative on a balance of probabilities for an activity to qualify as SR&ED.

The first criterion of the Northwest Hydraulic test asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Chief Justice Bowman held that the term "routine engineering" describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the relevant field. If the resolution of a problem is reasonably predictable using established methodologies, standard debugging, or off-the-shelf vendor documentation, no technological uncertainty exists—regardless of how complex, expensive, or commercially risky the project may be. Conversely, technological uncertainty arises when it is unknown whether a given objective can be achieved at all, or when the technical path to achieve it (such as reconciling competing system-level constraints like latency, memory footprint, and accuracy in an embedded algorithm) cannot be determined from publicly available scientific or engineering knowledge.

The second criterion asks whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. This requires an articulable scientific or engineering idea—consistent with known facts—posited at the outset of each iterative cycle as a testable causal proposition designed to resolve the identified technological obstacle. Flowing directly from hypothesis formulation, the third criterion asks whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Trial-and-error tinkering or intuition-driven coding fails this test; instead, the taxpayer must demonstrate a disciplined, five-stage methodological loop consisting of defining the problem and baseline knowledge, advancing a specific hypothesis, planning and executing controlled experiments or mathematical/computational analyses, systematically observing and measuring the results, and drawing logical conclusions that either validate the hypothesis or lead to its systematic modification for the next experimental iteration.

The fourth criterion asks whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. A technological advancement represents an advancement in the general understanding of science or technology relative to the baseline knowledge available to competent professionals at the start of the project—even if the advancement is incremental. Crucially, Chief Justice Bowman established that the rejection of a hypothesis is itself a technological advancement if it eliminates a plausible technical avenue and advances engineering knowledge of why a given approach fails under defined constraints. Finally, the fifth criterion asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed. Because scientific investigation is inherently iterative and evidence-based, a taxpayer claiming SR&ED must maintain contemporaneous records generated during the prosecution of the work—such as dated test logs, Git commit histories linked to experimental tickets, benchmark performance runs, failed prototype logs, and laboratory notebooks—rather than reconstructing technical narratives post-hoc for tax filing purposes.
Federal Court of Appeal Affirmations and the Status of CRA Administrative Guidelines

The five-question framework formulated in Northwest Hydraulic was elevated to binding national precedent by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, and consistently applied across subsequent decades by the Tax Court of Canada, including in Clevor Technologies Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2019 TCC 166 (per Justice Russell).

In August 2021, the CRA archived its legacy Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (which explicitly structured audit reviews around the five questions) and published simplified administrative guidelines organized around two overarching requirements: the "Why" Requirement (asking why the work is being conducted—namely, to advance scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement) and the "How" Requirement (asking how the work is being conducted—namely, by means of a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing hypothesis generation, testing, logical conclusions, and contemporaneous record-keeping).

Following this administrative shift, taxpayers questioned whether the CRA's two-question ("Why" and "How") framework altered the legal threshold for eligibility. The Federal Court of Appeal resolved this issue in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, building on its earlier decision in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88. The Federal Court of Appeal confirmed that CRA guidance, while useful context for understanding the purpose and intent of a provision, is not binding on the courts, and that the Tax Court made no error in relying on the five-question test established in Northwest Hydraulic to interpret subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. In practice, the CRA's "Why" requirement maps directly to Questions 1 and 4 of Northwest Hydraulic (Technological Uncertainty and Technological Advancement), while the "How" requirement maps directly to Questions 2, 3, and 5 (Hypothesis Formulation, Systematic Investigation, and Contemporaneous Evidence).
Recent Tax Court Jurisprudence and Evidentiary Standards

The enduring vitality of the Northwest Hydraulic criteria and the judicial approach to weighing technical evidence were vividly illustrated in the recent Tax Court of Canada decision in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (T.C.C., 2025). In that case, the appellant food-science enterprise claimed SR&ED expenditures for the 2020 taxation year in respect of experimental development undertaken to formulate and shelf-stabilize a novel beverage product ("Chrisoda"), which the Minister of National Revenue disallowed in full on the basis that the activities constituted routine food product development rather than SR&ED under subsection 248(1).

In allowing the taxpayer's appeal, the Tax Court of Canada systematically applied each of the five Northwest Hydraulic questions while reiterating Chief Justice Bowman's foundational interpretive principle (originally cited from Conoltex Inc.) that the SR&ED provisions of the Income Tax Act are intended to encourage scientific research in Canada and should be approached with a degree of practical realism rather than pedantic formalism. The Court emphasized two decisive evidentiary lessons for Canadian claimants: first, that merely facing an uncertain path toward a commercial product objective is insufficient on its own, as the taxpayer bears the legal burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that the underlying technical obstacle could not be resolved through routine engineering or standard procedures available in the industry; and second, that presenting credible, contemporaneous records of trained observation, quantitative measurement, and iterative hypothesis modification across successive experimental batches is decisive in discharging the burden of proof and overturning an administrative denial.
Strategic Compliance Conclusions and Audit Readiness Imperatives

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026—retroactively governing taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—combined with the launch of the CRA's Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026 and the implementation of Quebec's consolidated CRIC regime for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, fundamentally alters the strategic calculus for corporate R&D tax planning in Canada. To maximize non-dilutive capital recovery while insulating claims against CRA and provincial audit adjustments, Canadian enterprises and tax practitioners must integrate six rigorous operational protocols into their corporate tax governance.

First, qualifying CCPCs with prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeding $15,000,000 must model both the expanded taxable capital phase-out formula ($15 million to $75 million) and the new elective three-year average gross revenue phase-out formula ($15 million to $75 million) prior to filing Schedule T2SCH31, electing whichever metric maximizes access to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit and the $2,100,000 refundable ITC ceiling. Similarly, Canadian public corporations listed on designated stock exchanges must audit their shareholder registers and governance agreements to verify that they are not controlled directly or indirectly by non-resident persons, securing Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) status under the definition in subsection 127(9).

Second, corporate fixed-asset ledgers must segregate and track the exact acquisition date, available-for-use date, and 90% ("all or substantially all") SR&ED operating-time or value-consumption intent for all R&D equipment acquired after December 15, 2024. While these capital expenditures now qualify for the federal subsection 37(1) pool, the 35%/15% federal ITC (with 40% refundability at the 35% tier), Ontario's 8% OITC (for acquisitions on or after December 16, 2024), and Quebec's 30%/20% CRIC, claimants operating in Alberta must strictly exclude federal post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures by ensuring Line 003 of Alberta Form AT29 pulls exclusively from Line 557 (current expenditures) rather than Line 559 of federal Form T661.

Third, rather than defaulting to the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under Regulation 2900(4), compute-intensive artificial intelligence, data analytics, and biotechnology companies must perform annual arithmetic modelling comparing the 55% notional proxy (recognizing the exclusion of bonuses, taxable benefits, and specified employee amounts above 75% time and 2.5x YMPE) against actual, incremental cloud computing and laboratory infrastructure costs claimable under the Traditional Method before making the irrevocable annual election on Line 160 of Form T661.

Fourth, for capital-intensive or borderline experimental development initiatives, businesses should submit an application through My Business Account under the CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process launched on April 1, 2026, securing a binding eligibility determination from the CRA within eight weeks before committing substantial payroll or capital outlays. Fifth, because the Federal Court of Appeal in Kam-Press and National R&D confirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic five-question test remains the binding legal standard under subsection 248(1), technical teams must capture contemporaneous evidence of baseline knowledge limitations, explicit hypotheses, test failures, and quantitative results directly within daily engineering repositories (such as Jira, Git, and laboratory information management systems), ensuring seamless alignment with the word-capped narratives on Lines 242, 244, and 246 of Form T661. Finally, corporate tax departments must enforce strict calendar controls well ahead of the 18-month reporting deadline under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m), ensuring that all project descriptions, Schedule 31 calculations, Schedule 49 associated-group allocations, and non-arm's-length agreements (Forms T1145, T1146, and T1174) are accurately transmitted on the current 2026 revision of Form T661 before the statutory window permanently closes under subsection 220(2.2).
